assessment.nobel_worthiness: Grossman and Helpman built the standard framework for the political economy of trade protection (the 'protection for sale' model) and, with their work on innovation, trade and endogenous growth, shaped modern thinking on how policy is set under interest-group pressure. The contribution is foundational, conceptually general and has been used widely in applied work.
assessment.attribution: The two are the clear joint originators of both the protection-for-sale framework and the innovation-and-growth-in-open-economies synthesis. Helpman also appears on B008, but this entry is credited to the pair and does not need additional names.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s, has been tested and extended for decades, and is firmly part of textbooks and graduate training. Timing is not a constraint.
uncertainties: Empirical support for the specific protection-for-sale predictions is mixed.
The Committee may prefer to honour Helpman for firm heterogeneity (B008) instead, which could split support in trade.
I am relying on my own recollection of the literature rather than verified sources.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson, Tabellini and Besley developed modern political economics: how electoral rules and constitutions shape fiscal policy and public goods, and how state capacity develops. They gave the field a systematic theoretical and empirical base that links politics to economic outcomes and has influenced development, public finance and macroeconomics.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central authors of the constitutional and electoral-rules programme. Besley is closely tied to state capacity and to the political economy of development and accountability. The three together cover the field well.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and later, has a large body of replication and follow-up, and has been consolidated in textbooks and handbooks.
uncertainties: The recent Prizes on institutions and on growth through creative destruction may lower the room for a related award.
Persson's links to the Stockholm environment are a disclosed conflict, not an adjudicated one.
Credit relative to other political economists is a judgement call, and a three-name limit forces a choice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities, staggered pricing and interest-rate rules underlies modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. The Taylor rule, Calvo pricing and Woodford's theoretical synthesis are widely used in policy and research.
assessment.attribution: Credit is highly dispersed across many contributors (Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others). Calvo (pricing), Taylor (rules and staggered contracts) and Woodford (the microfounded synthesis) are the most separable foundations, but any three-name selection omits major contributors.
assessment.maturity: The framework has had decades of impact on policy and use in practice, so maturity is very high.
uncertainties: The attribution problem is severe given the number of strong contributors.
The framework has been challenged since the pandemic inflation episode and by heterogeneous-agent models (B018).
Part of the field overlaps with my own research area, so I discount my confidence in picking among colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Obstfeld and Rogoff brought intertemporal, microfounded analysis to open-economy macroeconomics (the 'Redux' model, their textbook) and documented the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles. The work gave the field its modern analytical base for international macroeconomic policy.
assessment.attribution: The pair is well defined as joint authors of the core framework and the standard graduate text. Rogoff also appears in B007 with Reinhart, which is a distinct contribution.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s, has been tested and refined for three decades and has wide policy use.
uncertainties: Some of the impact comes through the textbook and synthesis rather than a single empirical discovery.
The exchange-rate disconnect puzzles remain partly unresolved.
Rogoff's other work could create competing claims on credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work explains how technology and trade reshape labour demand and wage inequality: the task-based approach to skill-biased change and the 'China shock' evidence on local labour-market adjustment. It changed academic and policy debates on globalisation and automation.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both strands. Hanson is central to the trade-shock evidence, and Katz to the earlier skill-premium and technology-race work. Dorn is also a key co-author on the China shock, so the three-name limit leaves out a real contributor.
assessment.maturity: The task-based work has been important since the early 2000s and the China shock papers since 2013. The evidence base is large, though it is still being revised.
uncertainties: Parts of the empirical findings are still debated, especially on identification and long-run effects.
Credit is split among several authors and strands.
The China shock work is more recent than other candidates, though already influential.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore showed how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks through credit cycles. This became a base model for macro-finance and financial-crisis analysis, and it links asset prices, credit limits and real activity.
assessment.attribution: The 1997 Kiyotaki–Moore paper is a well-defined joint contribution. Gertler and Gilchrist are associated with the related financial accelerator literature, but the core of the collateral-constraint cycle model is attributable to the two.
assessment.maturity: The model dates from the 1990s, and its relevance was reinforced by the 2008 crisis and the subsequent literature, so it is mature.
uncertainties: The recent macro-finance work building on it is spread over many authors.
The Committee may prefer a broader award on financial frictions.
Overlap with the financial accelerator tradition could complicate attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work combined optimal-tax theory with empirical sufficient-statistic methods and administrative data, changing how tax policy is analysed in practice. The elasticity of taxable income and the optimal top-rate calculations have been influential in public economics.
assessment.attribution: Saez is the clearest central figure. Chetty is a leader in sufficient-statistic methods, but his most visible work also falls under B038 on mobility. Slemrod and Stantcheva are significant but harder to place within the three-name limit.
assessment.maturity: The empirical tax literature has built up over two decades and has strong policy impact. Some results are still debated.
uncertainties: Chetty is also a candidate in other entries, which may dilute or concentrate credit.
Elasticity estimates and optimal-tax conclusions remain contested.
Chetty's age and recency of his major contributions could affect timing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh and Klenow showed quantitatively how misallocation of inputs across firms can explain large cross-country differences in productivity and income. The paper became a standard tool for development and growth accounting, and it connects firm-level data to aggregate outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the authors of the core 2009 paper and its follow-ups. Restuccia and Rogerson are related contributors, and Restuccia is included in the credited list, so the two-name choice leaves out a legitimate contributor.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been used for roughly fifteen years with many extensions, so it is reasonably mature, though less seasoned than some other candidates.
uncertainties: Measurement of misallocation is sensitive to assumptions about markups and data quality, and critics have questioned its interpretation.
Credit relative to Restuccia and Rogerson is uncertain.
The contribution is more recent than that of other top-ranked candidates.
